newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - Gasoline, Iraq mold market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - Gasoline, Iraq mold market.

text.p: Gasoline prices are seen as the key barometer for gauging U.S. crude market direction this week, though the ever-present Iraq oil sales saga may throw off fundamentals, traders and analysts said Monday.
Analysts said early indications point to benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing testing downside support before a possible recovery later in the week.
"My feeling is that by the end of the week, we may not be too far from where we are now," said William Borwn, president of New York-based W.H. Brown & Co.
At 1245 EDT (1645 GMT), September NYMEX futures stood two cents lower at $19.87 a barrel.
Brown based his projection for a price ease on expectations for unfriendly gasoline inventory data releases this week, showing decreased demand numbers.
Besides the statistical probability for a negative turn for gasoline, Brown said spurt buying ahead of Hurricane Danny may have propped the market last week.

"There is probability for a drop in implied demand. I think this was delayed by the fact secondary stocks built ahead of Hurricane Danny as a precaution, and those demand levels were not sustainable," said Brown.

Grade traders active in the U.S. Gulf said rangebound pricing looked likely for this week, though some softness may be seen for sweet barrels on concerns refiners were well-supplied for the near-term.
Medium-term sour barrels were also under watch for softeness ahead of a possible influx of Iraqi crude after the second round of oil-for-food sales resume.

On the bullish side for sweet grades was the lack of interest for North Sea Brent barrels in the Gulf. Brent was notionally discussed at WTI minus 10-15 cents, an expensive level for most refiners, traders said.
The start to September business has quietly started at unchanged levels, with key sweet Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James holding a 20 cents edge over the benchmark.
West Texas Sour/Midland hovered around $1.65-55 under level, and Midland stuck at 30 cents below WTI/Cushing.
"The feature in there so far is that many people are out this week and likely to leave September business alone for the first few days of the week," a cash dealer said.
News focused squarely on the timing for resuming Iraqi oil sales under the stalled U.N. "oil-for-food" accord.

As of Monday morning, the U.N. was still waiting for final documentation related to Baghdad's aid distribution plan. Once the annexes to the main document are filed, the process of approving the aid plan, and triggering final implementation of the aid accord, can start in earnest.

Baghdad likely faces a daunting task in selling and exporting large volumes of oil ahead of a September 5 deadline for the first $1 billion worth of oil sales, as determined by the resolution governing the accord.
